newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria says Moslem rebels kill six civilians.
newsitem.headline: Algeria says Moslem rebels kill six civilians.

text.p: Algeria's security forces said on Tuesday Islamist rebels killed six civilians overnight in an Algiers suburb in the latest in a string of bloody attacks that have rocked the capital.

In a statement issued by the official Algerian news agency APS, they said "the six civilians were killed overnight by a group of terrorists" in Baraki suburb, but gave no other details. The security forces usually refer to Moslem rebels as terrorists.
The killings brought to more than 70 the number of civilians killed this month in attacks blamed on the guerrillas.

Algerian newspapers reported that a car bomb in the capital on Monday killed eight people and one said the blast made a mockery of government claims to have gained the upper hand in its battle against the rebels.
Security forces had put the toll at three dead and up to 20 wounded.
"The number of dead reached eight and scores of people were seriously wounded," said the Arab-language daily Al Khabar, quoting hospital sources.
The leading French-language newspaper El Watan, well informed on security matters, quoted a police officer at the scene as saying that eight people died and many were wounded.
Al Khabar, El Watan and other newspapers blamed the blast on the Moslem rebels but there has been no claim of responsibility.
The country's most ruthless group, the Armed Islamic Group (GIA), has in the past claimed responsibility for such attacks and vowed to carry out more.
More than 1,400 civilians have died in bomb attacks by fundamentalist rebels in the past two years, according to a government human rights body.
About 60,000 people have died in Algeria since 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election which radical Islamists were poised to win.

A senior French official said on Tuesday that a letter to President Jacques Chirac purporting to come from the GIA threatened to "continue" attacks in France unless he intervened to free a leader of the group awaiting execution in Algeria.

The letter did not specifically mention the December 3 rush-hour bombing of a commuter train at Paris' Port-Royal station, but made a reference to an unspecified recent event. Television reports said it was sent after that attack.
Monday's bomb in Algiers ripped through the commercial Larbi Ben Mehidi Street, destroying a cafe and badly damaging a pizzeria and a betting office, witnesses said.
Newspapers said the explosion hit at lunch hour when the street was bustling with workers, street vendors and thousands of passers-by. The area is known for small fast-food restaurants and shops.

Liberte newspaper, reporting that the car used in the blast was stolen in the Moslem guerrillas' Eucalyptus district south of Algiers, said the explosion made a mockery of authorities' claims of a crushing victory over the rebels.
"Should we compare the official speech and the reality of the security situation? Shall we note for the umpteenth time this discrepancy?" asked the newspaper.
El Watan, ridiculing the government over the security situation, wrote that "(Prime Minister) Ahmed Ouyahia walked in Tunis's streets and stated 'We triumphed over terrorism'."
Ouyahia was quoted on Sunday at the end of his visit to neighbouring Tunisia as saying that the government had defeated the guerrillas and "terrorism is living its latest convulsive moment".
